rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test temperature-dependent selectivity while keeping the gradient fixed, targeting the crowded cluster near 4.2–4.4 minutes. The current elution window leaves ample time margin for resolving these critical pairs.

Make the gradient shallower at the better-performing temperature to improve the remaining critical separation. The last peak at 6.58 minutes leaves room to gain resolution without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

Test the intermediate slope: the 10-minute gradient nearly resolves the later critical pair, while the 14-minute gradient comfortably resolves the earlier one. A 12-minute gradient may bring both above R = 1.5 with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is achieved; now test whether higher temperature shortens elution while preserving full resolution. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate the temperature effect on the two marginally resolved pairs.

Return to 55 C and raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek faster elution while retaining full resolution. Injection 4 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this run tests whether narrowing the gradient window improves its speed.
Slightly flatten the gradient to recover resolution of the remaining R = 1.29 pair while retaining the faster start. This may achieve full resolution with earlier final elution than injection 4.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity for a different route to full resolution with the shorter gradient, since local changes around 55 C trade off the two critical pairs. Injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C to move beyond the apparent selectivity crossover responsible for the near-coelution in injection 5. This explores a potentially much faster fully resolved method while preserving injection 4 as the maximum-score fallback.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a moderately longer gradient to redistribute the crowded middle peaks seen in injection 9. This explores the fast, high-temperature branch while retaining injection 4 as the fully resolved benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the remaining critical pair separates further on this fast, high-temperature branch. Monitor the first pair as well, since stronger initial solvent will compress early retention.

Test whether a shallower gradient resolves the critical cluster at 40 C, where temperature provides a different selectivity pattern. The expected final elution remains below 10 minutes, and injection 4 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Refine injection 7 by flattening the gradient one more step, aiming to lift its R = 1.47 pair above 1.5 while preserving the other critical separation. This could provide a second maximum-score method with greater resolution margin and final elution below 10 minutes.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 4's slope and temperature. Because its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this gradient ends, full resolution should be retained with a lower final organic fraction.

Test an intermediate temperature with a shorter gradient for a faster selectivity window not yet sampled. The maximum-score methods remain available; this run checks whether both critical separations can be maintained at substantially earlier elution.

Test whether lowering temperature shifts the crowded cluster into a better-resolved elution order at the faster gradient. This isolates temperature relative to injection 15 while retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score fallback.

Explore the lower-temperature side of the central cluster's elution-order crossover with a moderately shallow gradient. This may yield another fully resolved selectivity window below 10 minutes, providing a new starting point for shortening the separation.

Refine the fully resolved injection 13 with a slightly steeper, shorter gradient to reduce final elution time. Its critical resolutions of 1.67 and 1.58 suggest enough margin for this small slope increase while retaining maximum CRF.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction shifts the critical central pair at 40 C away from coelution while shortening retention. This combines a narrower gradient window with the lower-temperature selectivity branch; injection 4 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Increase the slope one grid step from the fully resolved injection 14 to test the speed limit near the best method. This should shorten final elution, though the R = 1.59 pair may become limiting; retain injection 4 if full resolution is lost.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to balance the two critical separations at the successful temperature. This refines the maximum-score region while checking whether stronger initial solvent offers useful resolution margin without pushing final elution beyond 10 minutes.

Flatten injection 21's gradient to improve its single unresolved pair, using the R = 1.76 margin in the other critical pair. Final elution should remain below 10 minutes, potentially yielding a fully resolved alternative with better minimum resolution.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 22 to bring its R = 1.41 pair above 1.5, while the other critical pair has useful margin at 1.74. This targets another maximum-score method with stronger minimum resolution and expected final elution below 10 minutes.

Shorten the programmed gradient to 8 minutes while preserving the slope of the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. The gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the expected last peak at 7.60 minutes, so maximum CRF should be retained.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower version of injection 23, aiming to balance its two critical resolutions with final elution predicted just below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 4 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
